Assignment 3 - Text Mining

Text Mining

Question 1

First, I counted the number of abstracts associated with each PubMed search term.

abstract_counts <- pubmed |>
  count(term, name = "number_of_abstracts") |>
  arrange(desc(number_of_abstracts))

abstract_counts |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Number of abstracts"),
    caption = "Number of abstracts associated with each search term"
  )
Number of abstracts associated with each search term
Search term Number of abstracts
covid 981
prostate cancer 787
preeclampsia 780
cystic fibrosis 376
meningitis 317

There are 3241 abstracts with nonmissing text in the dataset. The search term with the largest number of abstracts is covid, with 981 abstracts.

I next tokenized each abstract into individual words and counted the frequency of every token.

abstract_tokens <- pubmed |>
  select(abstract_id, term, abstract) |>
  unnest_tokens(word, abstract) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(word),
    str_detect(word, "[a-zA-Z]")
  )

token_counts <- abstract_tokens |>
  count(term, word, sort = TRUE)

top5_raw <- token_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(n)) |>
  ungroup()

top5_raw |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Token", "Count"),
    caption = "Five most common tokens for each search term"
  )
Five most common tokens for each search term

The unfiltered results are dominated by frequently used English words such as articles, conjunctions, and prepositions. These words occur often because of sentence structure, but they provide relatively little information about the scientific subjects of the abstracts. The results demonstrate why stop-word removal is an important preprocessing step in text mining.

Question 2

I removed common English stop words using the stop_words dataset supplied by the tidytext package.

tokens_without_stopwords <- abstract_tokens |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

clean_token_counts <- tokens_without_stopwords |>
  count(term, word, sort = TRUE)

top5_clean <- clean_token_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(n)) |>
  ungroup()

top5_clean |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Token", "Count"),
    caption = paste(
      "Five most common tokens for each search term after removing",
      "stop words"
    )
  )
Five most common tokens for each search term after removing stop words

Removing stop words substantially changes the most frequent tokens. The new lists contain more medically and scientifically meaningful terms that reflect the subjects represented by the PubMed searches. The highest-frequency non-stop-word token overall is covid, which occurs 7,275 times within the covid search group.

Question 3

I tokenized the abstracts into bigrams, meaning sequences of two consecutive words. I excluded bigrams in which both words were stop words. This retains phrases containing useful content while preventing combinations such as “of the” from dominating the results.

stop_word_vector <- stop_words |>
  distinct(word) |>
  pull(word)

bigram_counts <- pubmed |>
  select(abstract_id, term, abstract) |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, abstract, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  separate(
    bigram,
    into = c("word1", "word2"),
    sep = " ",
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(word1),
    !is.na(word2),
    str_detect(word1, "[a-zA-Z]"),
    str_detect(word2, "[a-zA-Z]"),
    !(word1 %in% stop_word_vector & word2 %in% stop_word_vector)
  ) |>
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE)

top10_bigrams <- bigram_counts |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)

top10_bigrams |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Bigram", "Count"),
    caption = "Ten most common bigrams"
  )
Ten most common bigrams
Bigram Count
prostate cancer 3222
pre eclampsia 1854
patients with 1587
of covid 1519
of prostate 870
cystic fibrosis 860
the covid 706
of pre 604
of preeclampsia 578
with covid 576 
top10_bigrams |>
  mutate(bigram = fct_reorder(bigram, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = bigram)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#990000", width = 0.75) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = comma(n)),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = comma,
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Most Common Bigrams",
    subtitle = "Bigrams containing two stop words were excluded",
    x = "Number of occurrences",
    y = NULL
  )

The most frequent bigram is “prostate cancer”, appearing 3,222 times. In contrast to the single-token analysis, the bigram analysis provides context by showing which words commonly occur together.

Question 4

For the TF-IDF analysis, each search term was treated as a document. Term frequency measures how frequently a token appears within a search term, while inverse document frequency gives greater weight to tokens that are uncommon across the other search terms.

tf_idf_results <- clean_token_counts |>
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = word,
    document = term,
    n = n
  )

top5_tf_idf <- tf_idf_results |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = tf_idf, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(tf_idf)) |>
  ungroup()

top5_tf_idf |>
  select(term, word, n, tf, idf, tf_idf) |>
  mutate(
    tf = round(tf, 5),
    idf = round(idf, 5),
    tf_idf = round(tf_idf, 5)
  ) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Search term",
      "Token",
      "Count",
      "Term frequency",
      "Inverse document frequency",
      "TF-IDF"
    ),
    caption = "Five tokens with the highest TF-IDF for each search term"
  )

The Question 1 results emphasize tokens that occur frequently, even if those tokens are common across several search groups. In comparison, TF-IDF emphasizes tokens that are both important within one search term and relatively uncommon in the other search terms. Therefore, the TF-IDF results are more useful for identifying words that distinguish one collection of abstracts from another.

Sentiment Analysis

Question 5

I used the NRC lexicon to classify words into the sentiments anger, anticipation, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, surprise, and trust, as well as the broader positive and negative categories.

nrc_lexicon <- get_sentiments("nrc")

nrc_counts <- tokens_without_stopwords |>
  inner_join(nrc_lexicon, by = "word") |>
  count(term, sentiment, sort = TRUE)

most_common_nrc <- nrc_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term) |>
  ungroup()

most_common_nrc |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Most common sentiment", "Count"),
    caption = "Most common NRC sentiment for each search term"
  )
Most common NRC sentiment for each search term
Search term Most common sentiment Count
covid positive 9254
cystic fibrosis positive 2564
meningitis negative 1959
preeclampsia positive 7603
prostate cancer negative 8799

When all NRC categories are retained, broad classifications such as positive or negative may be the most frequent because they apply to a large number of words. I therefore repeated the comparison after removing those two categories.

nrc_emotion_counts <- nrc_counts |>
  filter(!sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative"))

most_common_emotion <- nrc_emotion_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term) |>
  ungroup()

most_common_emotion |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Search term", "Most common emotion", "Count"),
    caption = paste(
      "Most common NRC sentiment after excluding positive and negative"
    )
  )
Most common NRC sentiment after excluding positive and negative
Search term Most common emotion Count
covid fear 7373
cystic fibrosis disgust 1714
meningitis fear 1371
preeclampsia anticipation 4555
prostate cancer fear 8039

Removing the positive and negative categories provides a more specific description of the emotions associated with the language in each group. The table shows which of the eight remaining NRC emotions is most common for each search term.

The following visualization displays all eight specific emotion categories.

nrc_emotion_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = sentiment,
      y = proportion,
      fill = sentiment
    )
  ) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "NRC Emotions in PubMed Abstracts",
    x = "Emotion",
    y = "Proportion of classified emotion words"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )

Question 6

Finally, I used the AFINN lexicon. AFINN assigns sentiment words integer scores ranging from negative values for negative words to positive values for positive words. I calculated the mean AFINN score among matched sentiment words in each abstract.

afinn_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "fnielsen/afinn/master/afinn/data/AFINN-111.txt"
)

afinn_lexicon <- read_tsv(
  afinn_url,
  col_names = c("word", "value"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

abstract_afinn <- abstract_tokens |>
  inner_join(afinn_lexicon, by = "word") |>
  group_by(abstract_id, term) |>
  summarise(
    average_positivity = mean(value),
    matched_words = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

afinn_summary <- abstract_afinn |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarise(
    abstracts_with_scored_words = n(),
    mean_score = mean(average_positivity),
    median_score = median(average_positivity),
    standard_deviation = sd(average_positivity),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_score))

afinn_summary |>
  mutate(
    mean_score = round(mean_score, 3),
    median_score = round(median_score, 3),
    standard_deviation = round(standard_deviation, 3)
  ) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Search term",
      "Abstracts with scored words",
      "Mean score",
      "Median score",
      "Standard deviation"
    ),
    caption = "Summary of average AFINN positivity scores"
  )
Summary of average AFINN positivity scores
Search term Abstracts with scored words Mean score Median score Standard deviation
cystic fibrosis 357 0.322 0.500 1.186
preeclampsia 769 -0.121 -0.143 0.918
covid 958 -0.147 -0.160 0.990
meningitis 292 -0.163 -0.211 1.183
prostate cancer 787 -0.239 -0.250 0.543 
abstract_afinn |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = fct_reorder(term, average_positivity, .fun = median),
      y = average_positivity,
      fill = term
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(
    alpha = 0.55,
    trim = FALSE,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.16,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.85,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray35"
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of AFINN Scores by Search Term",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Each score is the mean AFINN value among sentiment words",
      "in one abstract"
    ),
    x = "Search term",
    y = "Average positivity score"
  )

The group with the highest median positivity score is cystic fibrosis, with a median score of 0.5. The group with the lowest median score is prostate cancer, with a median score of -0.25.

The violin and box plots show both the centers and the distributions of the scores. Search terms whose boxes and median lines are noticeably higher or lower than those of the other groups have different sentiment patterns. However, these scores describe the language used in the abstracts and should not be interpreted as direct measurements of the authors’ emotions.
